# Design

Three waves. Wave 1 builds eleven foundations. The sidecar crate is laid down first - its configuration and its std-library HTTP server - and three tasks then fill it in parallel: fetch, extraction and the content digest; the crawler and the tantivy index; the 402LXP seller. Beside them, with no shared file, the xweb module is written with its request store, fulfilment, attestor set and governance messages, and the precompile and its Solidity interface are written against it; the kernel gains the web observation activity and then the web_read host import; the TypeScript and Python clients and the MCP tool are written against the sidecar's recorded 402 exchange; and the one workflow is added. Wave 2 integrates: the attestor signer and submitter close the contract loop, the program request path closes the kernel loop, the sidecar is packaged into its own image, a unit, a compose entry and the node image, the v6.8 upgrade plan wires the module and the precompile into the application, the documentation page is written, and a local dry run with anvil and local sidecars is recorded. Wave 3 runs the workflow's command set once on the merged revision and writes down what ran.

## The x-websearch sidecar

x-websearch is one binary with one configuration file. The configuration names the listen address, the data directory for the index and the content store, the seed list and the crawl budget, the fetch limits and the allow_loopback flag, the four accepted assets with their kernel asset ids and per-request prices, the gateway endpoint and the sequencer trust inputs for settlement, the EVM endpoint and chain id the attestor watches, the kernel network id, and the peer sidecars it exchanges signatures and content with. Keys never appear in it: the attestor key, the submitter key and the 402 receiver key are files named by environment variables. The loader decodes with unknown fields refused and refuses every placeholder, naming the field.

The HTTP server is a std::net::TcpListener with a bounded worker pool, request-line and header size limits, a read timeout and one response per connection. It serves GET /health free, and GET /search?q=, GET /fetch?url= and GET /content/<digest> as paid resources. An unpaid request receives 402 with PAYMENT-REQUIRED; a request carrying PAYMENT-SIGNATURE is settled through the seller and receives the resource with PAYMENT-RESPONSE, or a refusal naming the reason.

A fetch resolves the host, refuses a forbidden destination, checks robots.txt, follows at most three redirects under the same checks, reads at most 2 MiB within the time limits, extracts and canonicalises the text, and writes the canonical bytes to the content store under their digest so GET /content/<digest> can return them later; a digest the store does not hold is retrieved from the peer sidecars and kept only when its recomputed digest matches. The crawler walks the seed list inside its budget with the same fetch path, obeys robots.txt and the politeness delay, and writes url, title and body into the tantivy index; search queries it and returns at most ten results in the canonical order.

## Pay per request

Every paid route offers the same four assets. For each, the offer carries the metered scheme bound to a payer grant with one draw per request, and an exact alternative, both at the operator's price for that asset. The receiver identity signs the ordinal-6 draw, submits it to the gateway with lx_sendActivity at the offer's commitment, and releases the resource only when a receipt signed by the configured sequencer names the draw, the payer, the asset and the amount. A retry of the same request reuses the same signed activity and idempotency key; a pending result is recovered, never replaced; a receipt never releases a second request.

The price rule is written once in the documentation and in the configuration example: an operator sets each asset's price per request so that it equals one tenth of a US cent at the time of configuration. The committed example carries placeholders the loader refuses, so no sidecar starts with a price nobody chose.

## The xweb precompile and module

A contract calls request on the precompile at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001019 with the kind, the payload and the callback gas, paying exactly the current fee. The module checks it is not paused, the kind is known, the payload is within the payload cap and the callback gas within the callback cap, takes the fee into the module account, stores the request under the next nonce with the requester, the kind, the payload hash, the callback gas, the fee and the height, and emits XWebRequested with every field an attestor needs.

fulfil rebuilds the 188-byte origin-1 preimage from the stored request and the submitted response, digest and length, verifies the signatures with the bridge's verification shape, refuses a response longer than 4096 bytes, a length shorter than the response, a fulfilled or refunded request and a paused module, then stores the response, the digest and the length, marks the request fulfilled, pays the fee to the signers' payout accounts and calls the requester's onXWebResponse with the bounded gas. A reverting callback is recorded in the stored result and the fulfilment stands.

Governance holds the attestor set, the threshold with its majority rule, the fee, the payload and callback caps, the timeout and the pause, through messages carrying the gov authority in the shape of modules/layerxbridge/types/msgs.go. The precompile exposes the views a contract or an auditor needs: the request, the result, the attestor set, the threshold and the fee.

## The kernel path

The kernel learns a web observation activity beside the oracle push activity. Its payload is the origin-2 preimage fields, the stored response bytes and the signatures. Intake rebuilds the preimage, recovers each signer with lxp_secp256k1_recover_address, requires strictly ascending registered signers at the kernel web attestor threshold, requires a pending program web request with the same program id, request id, kind and payload hash, and commits the observation. The sequencer folds committed observations into a web root in the batch header the way lx_oracle_root.c folds oracle observations, so replay reproduces them.

A program asks for data by emitting a web request record through event_emit - a fixed topic defined in lx_web.h followed by the request id, the kind and the payload - and paying the web fee account with transfer_402 in the same call; the call bridge records the pending request only when both succeed. web_read takes a request id and an output buffer and returns the committed response, digest and length, or absent. It reads committed state only, so program execution never dials out.

Attestor sidecars watch program web request records through the gateway, fetch independently, sign the origin-2 digest, exchange signatures and post the observation activity once the threshold is reached, in the same encoding the C adapter produces, asserted byte for byte against a shared vector.
